title: Among the CCSPP schools, what are the academic, social-emotional, health, and family supports available to students and families?
text:
This section of the APR captures the range and alignment of academic, social-emotional, health, and family supports available to students and families. The questions are designed to assess how well these supports are coordinated and responsive to local needs and assets.
The 27 supports in the inventory are divided into six categories, according to the nature of the support: Integrated Student Supports and Services; Community, Student & Family Engagement; Collaborative Leadership Practices; Expanded & Enriched Learning Time; Community-based Curriculum & Pedagogy, and; Positive & Restorative School Climate. Each category is presented in a different section below. For each support identified under the category, grantees were asked to identify those that were part of their implementation plan.

title: Among the CCSPP schools, what are the academic, social-emotional, health, and family supports available to students and families?
text:
Cohorts 1-4, Year 4 Overview

Year 4 OnlyAcross Years


















I. Integrated Student Supports and Services


Highlights


Availability/PresenceImplementation of the Support/ServiceServed individuals by Support/ServiceSupport/Service Funding


In Year 4, including schools from Cohort 1 to Cohort 4, the supports that were more available in community schools in Integrated Student Support and Services were the Multi-Tiered System of Support, with 83% of schools reporting it as part of their implementation, and Mental Health Screening and Services, with 81% of schools reporting it as part of their implementation. Academic Support (tutoring, specialists, etc.) was the third most selected support, with 79% of schools reporting it as part of their implementation.







Most schools were already offering Integrated Student Supports and Services when applying to the grant, reporting that they integrated these supports into the community school work. For instance, 89% of schools reported that they previously implemented Multi-Tiered System of Support and 87% of schools reported previously implementing Mental Health Screening and Services.
Now, it is interesting to see that 26% of schools report that they started implementing the Coordination of Services Team (e.g., COST team) exclusively as a result of the CCSPP funding.







Grantees were asked the number of individuals that were served by each support. In Year 4 of the CCSPP Implementation Grant, for those supports that are grouped around the presence of integrated student supports and services, it is possible to see that the Multi-Tiered System of Support is reaching an average of 407.3 students per school and Mental Health Screening and Services is reaching an average of 241.4 students per school. With the state average across all public schools being around 550 to 600 students per school, the supports are reaching big portions of students in CCSPP community schools.







To fund these supports and services, grantees were asked to report funding sources beyond CCSPP to sustain the support long-term. Grantees tapped into traditional funding sources, such as LCFF to support their Multi-Tiered System of Support (33% of grantees) and Title I to support offerings of Academic Supports (22% of grantees).
It is interesting to note that a support as extensively provided as the Mental Health Screening and Services is being funded through many different sources, with no one being largely too salient: 18% of schools report using LCFF funds; 19% report using District funds, 14% report using general funds.











II. Community, Student, and Family Engagement


Highlights


Availability/PresenceImplementation of the Support/ServicesServed individuals by Support/ServiceSupport/Service Funding


For supports that are categorized as Community, Student, and Family Engagement supports/services, 87% of grantees indicated implementing Multiple Modes of Family Communication and Involvement. In addition, 65% of schools indicated that they were implementing Home Visits in Year 4.







Grantee schools indicated that providing supports and services that aimed to engage students, families, and community was integrated into their community schools work. For Adult Education, over one-third of grantees (35%) indicated that the provision of Adult Education programs was made possible exclusively through CCSPP funding.







Grantees were asked the number of individuals that were served by each support. In Year 4 of the CCSPP Implementation Grant, for those supports that are grouped around Community, Student, and Family Engagement, it is possible to see that schools are reaching students’ parents and family members by communicating, visiting them, and engaging in formal education opportunities.







For those supports/services that are categorized under Community, Student, and Family Engagement, multiple sources of funding are used. For example, for family communication and engagement, percentages of schools reporting sources are 24% for LCFF, 23% for General Funds, and 19% for District Funds. Similar numbers for Home Visits. For Adult Education, however, Other sources are more generally reported (9%).











III. Collaborative Leadership Practices


Highlights


Availability/Presence of the Support/ServiceImplementation of the Support/ServicesServed individuals by Support/ServiceSupport/Service Funding


For those supports/services that are grouped under the category of Collaborative Leadership Practices, 86% of grantees have implemented and formed a shared decision-making body that aims to center the voices of all community members, including students, families, and other interest-holders.







For those supports that are grouped under the category of Collaborative Leadership practices, 30% of grantees started implementing Parent Leadership Development Opportunities exclusively because of CCSPP funding. In addition, 23% of grantees mentioned starting the Shared decision-making bodies exclusively as a result of CCSPP funding.







Grantee school sites were asked the number of individuals that were served by each support. For those supports that are grouped under Collaborative Leadership Practices, it is possible to see that parents and family members are being reached through Development Opportunities and Shared Decision-Making Bodies.







For those supports that are grouped under Collaborative Leadership Practices, Teacher Leadership Development and Opportunities are being funded by a diversity of sources –such as LCFF, General Funds, Title I, among others. In addition, newly implemented Shared Decision-Making Bodies are being funded by many sources, including the LCFF, General Funds, Title I funds, and District Funds.











IV. Expanded and Enriched Learning Time


Highlights


Presence of the Supports/ServicesImplementation of the Support/ServicesServed individuals by Support/ServiceSupport/Service Funding


For those supports that are grouped under the category of Expanded and Enriched Learning Time, 75% of grantees implemented After School programs. In addition, over 60% of schools have responded that they implemented Summer Programs and During School additional Programs.







For those support/services that are grouped under the category of Expanded and Enriched Learning Time, 19% of grantees mention starting Before School programs exclusively as a result of CCSPP funding. Also, at least 10% of schools providing After School programs and During School programs have started these thanks to the CCSPP funding.







For those supports/services that are grouped under the category of Expanded and Enriched Learning Time, it is possible to see that many students are being served by the programs implemented through the CCSPP funding.







For those supports that are grouped under the category of Expanded and Enriched Learning Time, Expanded Learning Opportunities Program (ELOP) is the main funding source for After School programs and Summer Programs, with 54% of schools mentioning they use these funds for After School programs and 40% of schools responding they use these funds for Summer Programs.











V. Community-based Curriculum and Pedagogy


Highlights


Availability/Overview of the Presence of the Support/ServiceImplementation of the Support/ServicesServed individuals by Support/ServiceSupport/Service Funding


For those supports that fall under the category of Community-based Curriculum and Pedagogy Practices, 52% of grantees mention implementing a Culturally-Sustaining and Responsive Curriculum and Pedagogy.







For those supports that are categorized under Community-based Curriculum and Pedagogy Practices, 30% of grantees mention that they started implementing Community-Based Curriculum, Pedagogy, and Projects exclusively as a result of the CCSPP funding. And 21% responded that they have started implementing Project-Based Learning thanks to the support CCSPP provides.







For those supports that are grouped under the category of Community-based Curriculum and Pedagogy Practices, each support is reaching hundreds of students across schools. On average, supports like Advisory Systems reach almost 400 students.







For those supports that are categorized under Community-based Curriculum and Pedagogy Practices, APR responses show that grantees are using a diversity of funding sources. In particular, General Funds, LCFF, and District funds are used to implement Project-Based Learning and Personalized Learning Plans.











VI. Positive and Restorative School Climate


Highlights


Availability/Overview of the Presence of the Support/ServiceImplementation of the Support/ServicesServed individuals by Support/ServiceSupport/Service Funding


For those supports/services that are categorized under Positive and Restorative School Climate, 83% of grantees mention implementing Positive Behavioral Supports and 84% responded that they are implementing Programs and Practices that Teach Social-Emotional Skills.







Grantees were asked when they started implementing each support. For those supports that are grouped under Positive and Restorative School Climate, 15% of grantees mention that the Programs and Practices that Teach Social-Emotional Skills that they implemented started exclusively as a result of CCSPP funding.







For those supports around Programs and Practices that Teach Social-Emotional Skills, on average, they are reaching around 470 students in each community school.







For those supports that are grouped under Positive and Restorative School Climate, it is possible to see that grantees are mainly using the LCFF as the main source to fund supports related to Positive Behavioral Supports, Practices that prevent, reduce, and eliminate exclusionary discipline, and Programs and practices that teach socio-emotional skills. 33% of schools responded using LCFF funds for the first group of supports, 26% for the second, and 30% for the third group.

title: Observed Improvements in School Climate
text:
Overview
QID172 asked grantees:

What improvements in school climate have you observed since the implementation of your CCSPP grant that you believe are connected to CCSPP activities? Please describe. (up to 300 words)

This page summarizes 1,863 usable responses from 2,381 schools in the 2025–26 APR. Responses had a median length of 221 words.






NoteWho answered this question



QID172 was shown only to schools that answered Strongly agree or Somewhat agree to “Our school climate has improved” (QID171). The 484 schools that were neutral or disagreed did not see the question, so these results describe how schools that saw improvement explain it. They cannot tell us why some schools did not.



Key takeaways

Schools mostly describe climate as relationships. Family engagement (83%), belonging (77%) and student–staff relationships (68%) are the most common themes.
SEL and mental health supports are the main mechanism named. “Social emotional” appears in 35% of responses, “mental health” in 21% and “restorative practices” in 16%.
Few responses give measurable evidence. Only 22% include a percentage. Named data sources are rare: CHKS 5%, Panorama 6%, CA Dashboard 2%.
Student voice is the least-mentioned theme (23%), even though it is central to the community schools framework.

Family engagement

title: Observed Improvements in School Climate
text:
How schools support their claims








Figure 7: Share of responses with each type of evidence.





About half of responses mention surveys or data in some form, but far fewer report a specific result. Only 13% describe fewer suspensions, referrals or incidents, and 17% describe better attendance. Roughly 29% rely on what staff have “observed” or “noticed,” and 12% acknowledge any challenge or mixed result.
The examples below show the range, from specific data to general statements.

Specific dataGeneral claim, no dataMixed results


A minority of responses give before-and-after figures from a named source:

Complementing these efforts, California Dashboard results show a reduction in chronic absenteeism from 41.5% to 35.7% and a decrease in suspension rates from 5.4% to 4.7%.
— Cohort 4 · Capitol Area · Strongly agree


CHKS data shows school connectedness rising to roughly 50% (from 39% in 2023), academic motivation near 62%, perceived safety near 59%, and an increased sense of belonging, alongside a declining suspension rate (2.5%, Green) and improving attendance.
— Cohort 3 · Southern Inland · Somewhat agree



More often, a response ends with a broad summary statement and no figures:

These combined efforts have contributed to a more inclusive, relationship-centered school culture where students and families feel increasingly connected, supported, and valued.
— Cohort 3 · Southern Coast · Somewhat agree



A few schools report declines or weak areas alongside their gains, even though they agreed climate improved:

School climate scores among students in grades 3–6 declined slightly from 49% to 47% favorable on the Panorama School Climate measure, and suspension rates remain at Orange on the CA Dashboard for multiple subgroups.
— Cohort 4 · Central Coast · Somewhat agree


However, Self-Efficacy ranks around the 20th percentile nationally with a 40% favorable response rate and a 5-point decline, suggesting students struggle with confidence in their academic abilities.
— Cohort 3 · Bay Area · Somewhat agree




This points to a technical assistance opportunity: helping schools connect climate claims to the survey and dashboard data they already collect.

title: Observed Improvements in School Climate
text:
Methods






CautionLimitations






Keyword coding, not human coding. Themes are flagged by keyword patterns. They are a transparent first pass and will miss paraphrases and include some false matches.
Only agreeing schools answered. See the note in the Overview.
Copied text. 119 responses (6.4%) exactly match another school’s text across 36 groups, usually district-level boilerplate. They are included here; setting drop_duplicates <- TRUE removes them.
Cohort 4 is underrepresented. Only about half of Cohort 4 schools answered QID172, because many were neutral on QID171. Cohort 4 results describe the schools that already see improvement.




Processing steps

Loaded the APR 2025–26 export through the shared prep script (00-prepare-climate-data.R), the same data used on the School Climate dashboard, keeping the 2,381 schools with a valid cohort, region and CDS code.
Dropped blank and placeholder answers (e.g., “N/A”).
Tokenized with tidytext, removed standard English stop words plus words that echo the prompt, and merged common singular/plural forms.
Counted each word and two-word phrase, both total mentions and the number of responses using it.
Flagged themes and evidence types using the keyword patterns below.
Selected example quotes by hand from responses that match each theme, leaving out copied (duplicate) responses and sentences that name a school. Each excerpt is stored with its Qualtrics ResponseId, and the page will not render unless every excerpt appears word for word in that response.

title: What are some of the effective practices schools are implementing?
text: 576 CCSPP schools from Cohorts 1-3, shared their best practices regarding community schools implementation, particularly the Capacity-Building Strategies, the engagement of educational partners and the provision of whole-child and family supports. The frequency visualization, below, highlights the most common areas of work where grantees are seeing promising progress.

title: Past APR Reports
text: This site presents findings from the current (Year 4, 2025-26) Annual Progress Report. Findings from earlier years are archived on their own sites, linked below.

title: What goals are grantees prioritizing and how are they making progress in meeting these goals?
text:
This section of the APR documents how grantees translate community priorities into clear goals and aligned actions. The questions assess the coherence, intentionality, and feasibility of planned implementation strategies.
As indicated in the CCSPP application and implementation process, schools are expected to prioritize the key topics, goals, and challenges identified in their Needs and Assets Assessment. As part of the APR, grantees were asked to submit their top three goals associated with their CCSPP implementation, in alignment with the California Community Schools Framework and the Whole Child and Family Supports Inventory.
CCSPP sites were asked to share the metrics associated with each of their school-specific goals. The most common metric selected was “other locally developed metric” (30% of the schools chose this option). Other common metrics included chronic absenteeism rates, climate measures and proficiency scores.
Within the category of “other” local measures, some common metrics were: service participation rates, socio-emotional learning surveys, school-developed surveys, family engagement, PBIS Tiered Fidelity Inventory scores, California State Seal of Civic Engagement, community partnerships growth, staff hiring and retention, among many others.
CCSPP sites also described the actions that they took to accomplish their goals. For those schools focused on improving student attendance and reducing chronic absenteeism, the top five actions that proved successful to advance this goal were:

title: Are CCSPP grantees building their capacity to implement the approach?
text:
The Capacity-Building Strategies (CBS) are crucial for enhancing the readiness and capability of all interest-holders and empowering them with the knowledge, skills, resources, and support to successfully translate the promise of Community Schools into practice. The Capacity-Building Strategies integrate the pillars, key conditions of learning, cornerstone commitments, and proven practices that comprise the CA CS Framework. They provide the road map or the “how” to bring the CA CS Framework to life.
The Capacity-Building Strategies are structured by three sequential phases of growth and development (visioning, engaging and transforming), each consisting of a set of activities designed to put Community Schooling into practice.
Across the State, the area with most grantees in the transforming phase is “Strategic Community Partnerships”: a fifth of the CCSPP schools are expanding access to services through well-established partnerships. Over 70% of the CCSPP schools are either in the engaging or transforming phases across all capacity building strategies, with the exception of centering community based learning, which continues to be an area of growth. That said, Cohort 1, for example, has seen a steady growth in this area, with 18% of schools in the transforming and 62% in the engaging phase for community based learning.
Community Schools are dynamic and seek to continuously evolve and grow, and thus perpetual reflection informs each phase of growth and development around these five strategies. Across the State, CCSPP have continued developing the core organizational, relational, and leadership capacities needed to implement and sustain the community school strategy. In the last school year, Cohort 1 experienced the highest average change in phases of growth in the areas of Collaborative Leadership (0.17) and Strategic Partnerships (0.17), closely followed by Community Based Learning (0.16). Cohort 2 also had the highest average growth in Strategic Partnerships (0.41), while Cohort 3 had the highest growth in Shared commitment, Understanding and Priorities (0.49).
Because change is complex, schools are not expected to progress in the capacity building strategies in a straight line. Schools may return to earlier strategies, adjust their approach, and move through the stages in different ways, depending on their needs and context. This process is often ongoing and flexible. For Cohort 3 schools, 39-50% of them grew in their phase of growth and development during their first year of implementation (24-25 to 25-26). Schools in other cohorts also improved consistently in their implementation of the capacity building strategies.

title: Are LEA-Level CCSPP grantees building their capacity to implement the approach?
text:
Figure 2 shows Cohort 1 LEA CBS ratings from all available valid responses in each year: 48 LEAs in 2023-24, 51-52 in 2024-25, and 55-56 in 2025-26. These are implementation years 2, 3, and 4 for Cohort 1. Because the group of responding LEAs changes from year to year, the figure describes the cohort as reported in each year, and year-to-year differences can reflect both changes in ratings and changes in who responded.
Between 2023-24 and 2025-26, the Visioning share declined and the Transforming share increased in all five strategies. Visioning fell from 37.5% to 7.1% in Shared Commitment, Understanding, and Priorities, from 41.7% to 10.9% in Collaborative Leadership, and from 25.0% to 3.6% in Strategic Community Partnerships. Transforming more than tripled in Shared Commitment (8.3% to 28.6%) and rose from 4.2% to 23.2% in Sustaining Staff and Resources. Strategic Community Partnerships remained the most advanced strategy by this measure, with Transforming increasing from 18.8% to 35.7%.
Most of the latest-year change occurred at the upper end of the scale. In 2024-25, Engaging accounted for 67.3% to 78.4% of ratings in four of the five strategies. From 2024-25 to 2025-26, Engaging declined and Transforming increased in every strategy. Sustaining Staff and Resources was the only strategy in which Visioning did not continue to decline, edging up from 11.5% to 12.5%. Centering Community-Based Learning progressed more slowly: Visioning declined from 52.1% to 29.1% over the three years but remained the highest Visioning share of any strategy in 2025-26, and Transforming reached 16.4%. Overall, the reported distribution moved toward later phases, although community-based learning remains a comparatively early area of implementation for this cohort.
Figure 2. Cohort 1 annual available-sample distributions. Changes may reflect both ratings and respondent composition.
Figure 3 shows all available valid Cohort 2 responses: 78 per item in 2023-24, 80-81 in 2024-25, and 84 in 2025-26. These are Cohort 2’s first three implementation years, so the figure follows the cohort from its start. As with Cohort 1, respondent membership varies across years, and differences can reflect both changes in ratings and changes in who responded.
In 2023-24, between 48.7% and 71.8% of ratings in each strategy were Visioning, and Transforming did not exceed 5.1% in any strategy. By 2025-26, Visioning had declined to below 10% in four strategies: Shared Commitment, Understanding, and Priorities (61.5% to 3.6%), Collaborative Leadership (67.9% to 9.5%), Sustaining Staff and Resources (48.7% to 4.8%), and Strategic Community Partnerships (48.7% to 3.6%). Engaging was the largest category in every strategy in 2025-26, ranging from 63.1% to 81.0%.
The timing of change differed across years. Between 2023-24 and 2024-25, movement was mainly from Visioning into Engaging, and Transforming remained at or below 10% in every strategy. Transforming grew mainly in the latest year: from 9.9% to 33.3% in Strategic Community Partnerships, from 7.4% to 17.9% in Collaborative Leadership, and from 1.2% to 17.9% in Sustaining Staff and Resources. Centering Community-Based Learning moved more slowly. Visioning declined from 71.8% to 27.4% and Engaging rose from 26.9% to 67.9%, but Transforming reached only 4.8% in 2025-26, so progress in this strategy mostly reflects movement into Engaging. In 2025-26, Cohort 2’s Transforming shares were lower than Cohort 1’s in every strategy; that year was Cohort 2’s third implementation year and Cohort 1’s fourth.
Figure 3. Cohort 2 annual available-sample distributions. These are implementation years 1, 2, and 3 for Cohort 2.

title: Are LEA-Level CCSPP grantees building their capacity to implement the approach?
section: Snapshot of Cohorts 1 through 4 in 2025 to 2026
text:
Snapshot of Cohorts 1 through 4 in 2025 to 2026
In the Year 4 APR (2025-26), LEAs serving Cohorts 1-3 most often rated their implementation as Engaging across all five Capacity-Building Strategies (CBSs). Cohort 1 had the largest Transforming share in each strategy. Strategic Community Partnerships had the highest Transforming share within every cohort: 35.7%, 33.3%, 18.1%, and 11.1% in Cohorts 1-4, respectively.
Centering Community-Based Learning had the highest Visioning share within each cohort: 29.1%, 27.4%, 36.1%, and 61.1%, respectively. Cohort 4 had a majority in Visioning only for this strategy; Engaging was its largest category in the other four. These distributions identify community-based learning as a comparatively early area of implementation, which is consistent with the site level findings.

Figure 1. LEA self-assessments across all five CBSs and all four cohorts in 2025-26.

title: Are LEA-Level CCSPP grantees building their capacity to implement the approach?
text:
Implementation across the five strategies
The following excerpts illustrate reported practices and challenges across five different LEAs. They were selected for relevance to each strategy, not through systematic qualitative coding, and do not establish how common a practice is. Phase labels refer to each LEA’s rating of the strategy discussed.

title: Are LEA-Level CCSPP grantees building their capacity to implement the approach?
text:
Shared Commitment, Understanding, and Priorities
Engaging accounted for 64.3% of Cohort 1, 81.0% of Cohort 2, 80.7% of Cohort 3, and 61.1% of Cohort 4 ratings in 2025-26. Transforming was most common in Cohort 1 (28.6%), while 36.1% of Cohort 4 remained in Visioning. In the three-year matched panels, Visioning declined from 36.6% to 2.4% in Cohort 1 and from 60.0% to 4.3% in Cohort 2. The distributions suggest that shared priorities are increasingly being put into practice among continuing respondents.

With respect to Shared Commitment, Understanding, and Priorities, the CCSPP enabled us to conduct structured focus groups with school staff, students, and families across sites, while establishing an LEA Steering Committee that now meets regularly.

Cohort 4; Visioning for this strategy. 2025-26 APR, CBS reflection.

title: Are LEA-Level CCSPP grantees building their capacity to implement the approach?
text:
Collaborative Leadership
Engaging was the most common phase in all four cohorts in 2025-26. Transforming ranged from 27.3% in Cohort 1 and 17.9% in Cohort 2 to 9.6% in Cohort 3 and 2.8% in Cohort 4. Within the matched panels, Visioning declined from 41.5% to 9.8% in Cohort 1 and from 68.6% to 7.1% in Cohort 2 between 2023-24 and 2025-26. These ratings describe broader adoption of collaborative leadership, while the reflection below gives one example of the structures LEAs associate with this work.

Through Collaborative Leadership, we continued to strengthen shared decision-making structures such as School Site Councils, English Learner Advisory Councils, Community School committees, and site leadership teams.

Cohort 2; Transforming for this strategy. 2025-26 APR, CBS reflection.
The example connects reported leadership capacity to recurring councils and committees involving families, educators, and community members.

title: Are LEA-Level CCSPP grantees building their capacity to implement the approach?
text:
Centering Community-Based Learning
Community-based learning had the highest Visioning share within every cohort in 2025-26. Even among Cohorts 1 and 2, 29.1% and 27.4% of annual respondents remained in Visioning. There was nonetheless movement in both matched panels: Cohort 1 Transforming increased from 2.4% to 12.2%, while Cohort 2 Engaging rose from 28.6% to 71.4% over the three years. San Diego Unified described professional learning and compensated collaboration time as supports for instructional change.

The CCSPP has provided the resources necessary for crucial support positions, along with time for educators to create, innovate, plan, and collaborate.

Cohort 1, Cohort 2, Cohort 3; Engaging for this strategy. 2025-26 APR, CBS reflection.
The example highlights protected collaboration time and staff support as part of the district’s approach to developing community-based learning.

title: Are LEA-Level CCSPP grantees building their capacity to implement the approach?
text:
Sustaining Staff and Resources
Engaging was the largest category in all four cohorts, ranging from 54.2% in Cohort 4 to 77.4% in Cohort 2. Cohort 1 had the largest Transforming share (23.2%). The matched panels showed higher Transforming shares in 2025-26 than in 2023-24: from 2.4% to 19.5% in Cohort 1 and from 1.4% to 18.6% in Cohort 2. Annual distributions add nuance: Cohort 1 Visioning increased slightly from 11.5% to 12.5% between 2024-25 and 2025-26, even as its Transforming share increased. Different respondent composition can contribute to differences between the annual and matched results.

Budget uncertainty and staffing stability remained sustainability concerns, especially when CCSPP-funded positions such as Community School Managers served as the connective link for coordinating partnership, services, and leadership teams.

Cohort 1, Cohort 2, Cohort 3; Engaging for this strategy. 2025-26 APR, CBS reflection.
Oakland’s reflection cautions against treating active staffing and coordination as proof that long-term funding is already secure.

title: Are LEA-Level CCSPP grantees building their capacity to implement the approach?
text:
Strategic Community Partnerships
Partnerships had the highest Transforming share within every cohort in 2025-26. Engaging remained the largest category, including in Cohort 1 (60.7% Engaging versus 35.7% Transforming). In the matched panels, Transforming increased from 19.5% to 36.6% in Cohort 1 and from 5.7% to 38.6% in Cohort 2 over the three years. These are changes in the same LEAs’ self-assessments. One LEA described one way its partnership work was organized:

standardized partnership tracking; and QR-coded Resource Hubs at every campus connecting families to mental health, nutrition, housing, and postsecondary supports.

Cohort 3; Transforming for this strategy. 2025-26 APR, CBS reflection.
The example connects partnership coordination with visible routes for families to reach services and postsecondary supports.
Taken together, the ratings and examples suggest useful questions for technical assistance: how LEAs support community-based learning within instruction, how shared leadership structures distribute influence, and how staffing plans connect to sustained funding.

title: To what extent are schools engaging key interest-holders in community schools implementation?
text:
This section of the APR examines how community schools engage various interest-holder groups in the process of implementation. The questions focus on the depth and quality of engagement with individuals such as students, staff, families members, and community partners.
Analysis of Year 4 APR data indicates that schools were most successful in engaging administrators (80% at 75-100% engagement rate), followed by certificated staff (47% at 75-100% engagement rate) and students (39% at 75-100% engagement rate). Classified staff (29%) and community partners (24%) saw comparatively lower rates of high engagement, and family members had the lowest share of schools reporting 75-100% engagement (19%). At the lower end, 3% of schools reported 0% engagement of community partners, and roughly one in five schools engaged community partners (38%) or family members (27%) at only a 1-24% rate.
Analysis of Year 4 APR data indicates that schools were most successful in engaging socioeconomically disadvantaged students (54% at 75-100% engagement rate) and racially marginalized populations (44% at 75-100% engagement rate) in developing their community schools. English language learners and chronically absent students saw more moderate engagement, with 30% and 26% of schools respectively reporting 75-100% engagement. Foster youth and homeless youth remained the least-engaged groups: only 25% of schools reported 75-100% engagement for either group, and both had the highest rates of 0% engagement (12% for foster youth, 6% for homeless youth). Foster youth also had the highest share of “not applicable” responses (5%) and non-responses (3%).
Qualitative analysis revealed three themes in schools’ approaches to engage marginalized groups: nearly half of schools (45.5%) mentioned some form of survey as their engagement strategy, a quarter describe providing basic-needs support (food, clothing, transportation). Schools also described how they employ individualized strategies: home visits, case management, one-on-one check-ins, and liaisons, specifically for the highest-need subgroups (homeless, foster, and chronically absent students).
Schools with higher self-reported engagement levels were meaningfully more likely to use case management and empathy interviews (6% vs. 3%), and were three times less likely to explicitly use “not yet started” or “still developing” language than low-engagement schools, suggesting that individualized, relationship-based methods (not just having more surveys and programs) are what distinguishes deepened implementation/engagement.

title: California Community Schools Partnership Program Annual Progress Report
text:
The Annual Progress Report (APR) serves as a tool to assess implementation progress and efforts, and to encourage reflection as part of an ongoing continuous improvement process. The APR was designed to be filled out by each school’s California Community Schools Partnership Program (CCSPP) shared decision-making team or council to ensure the perspectives of students, staff, families and community partners are captured. The reporting portal is intended to align with required annual update presentations on community school planning, including data and outcomes from the prior year at each school site.
The APR is aligned with the California Community Schools Framework and also aligns with resources provided by the State Transformational Assistance Center (S-TAC) listed in the side bar.
The visualizations and tables throughout this site reflect the data from the CCSPP APR for school sites for Year 1 (2022-2023), Year 2 (2023- 2024), and Year 3 (2024-2025) school years.

title: What are the identified needs and next steps based on a review of data?
text:
What are the identified needs and next steps based on a review of data?

LEAs were asked to describe 1) any areas that need significant improvement based on a review of the site-level APRs, and outcome data, Dashboard indicators, and 2) any steps taken to address those areas.
In Year 3, cohort 1-3 LEAs described using California School Dashboard indicators and local data (local assessments, surveys, and site-level program narratives) to identify persistent gaps and to prioritize a small set of outcomes for improvement. Overall, reflections show a consistent improvement approach: focus on high-leverage outcomes (especially attendance and academic performance) while strengthening the enabling systems—data routines, tiered supports, cross-role coordination, partnerships, and family engagement—needed to make progress sustainable.

Areas of need identified by LEAs:
Attendance and chronic absenteeism was frequently described as a “root” issue because it limits access to instruction and to community school supports. Responses connected attendance challenges to broader barriers (e.g., transportation and housing instability) and to equity concerns for prioritized student groups. Several LEAs described strengthening early identification, outreach, and follow-up (including case management approaches), emphasizing relationship-based strategies to understand barriers and re-engage families. “These efforts have helped build trust, identify root causes of absenteeism, and connect families to needed services and supports.”
Academic performance in ELA/literacy and math was often paired with concerns about persistent subgroup gaps. Steps taken commonly included strengthening intervention systems and expanding targeted supports (e.g., tutoring, small-group supports, extended learning), along with adult learning supports (professional learning, coaching, and instructional alignment) to improve implementation quality. “While proficiency rates remain a challenge, all sites have reported incremental gains, with coordinated tutoring programs, targeted workshops, and growth-focused incentives contributing to students’ academic development.”
Student well-being, mental health/SEL, school climate, and behavior/discipline were areas where needs remain high and often intertwined with attendance and academic outcomes. A recurring theme is that demand for mental health and counseling support exceeds current capacity. One response illustrates this gap between need and service reach: “Counseling services reached 45 students, though 157 referrals signaled a higher need.”
Data use and progress monitoring were emphasized by LEAs as the mechanism that links “identified needs” to concrete action—strengthening how teams review evidence, set priorities, coordinate across roles, and monitor whether strategies are working. “Schools are deepening their understanding of evidence-based practices and improving use of data to guide decisions.”
Year 3 reflections indicate that LEAs are aligning improvement efforts around a consistent set of outcomes—attendance, ELA/literacy, math, and student well-being/climate—while investing in the systems and routines (data cycles, tiered supports, coordination, and partnerships) that help translate identified needs into sustained action.

title: To what extent are LEAs engaging system-level activities to coordinate community school support?
text:
In this section of the LEA-level APR, LEAs were asked about the systems-level infrastructure and coordination supports they have in place to advance community schools implementation. Specifically, LEAs reported the extent to which they engage in a set of systems-level coordination activities—such as learning and reflection through a steering committee/advisory council, policy alignment, data systems for continuous improvement, professional learning supports, sustainability planning, and coordination with external partners.
Across all 3 cohorts, most LEAs report developing systems to support school capacity to access, understand, and use data for continuous program improvement (82%–91% medium/large extent) and pursuing policy initiatives that align with and reinforce the shared vision for community schooling (77%–88% medium/large extent). Findings also show strong external coordination, particularly for newer cohorts: Cohort 2 and Cohort 3 report higher “large extent” engagement with R‑TACs and County Offices of Education than Cohort 1. One area that remains less developed across cohorts is establishing a structure for cross-sector problem-solving of system-level barriers, where only about half of LEAs report engaging in this work to medium/large extent—an important opportunity for strengthening system conditions that can sustain community school implementation over time. These findings demonstrate that LEAs are working to build system-wide infrastructures to support the capacity-building of interest-holders.
